overview: Oxygen tolerance shapes how an organism generates energy and how it must be cultured in the lab.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: Bacteria that require oxygen for growth, using it as the final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration.
aspects.valueB: Bacteria that grow without oxygen; many are actively harmed or killed by it.

aspects.label: Oxygen Requirement
aspects.valueA: Obligate aerobes need atmospheric O2; some are facultative and can also grow without it.
aspects.valueB: Obligate anaerobes cannot tolerate O2; some are aerotolerant and survive brief exposure without using it.

aspects.label: Energy Metabolism
aspects.valueA: Aerobic respiration, with oxygen as the terminal electron acceptor and a full electron transport chain.
aspects.valueB: Fermentation or anaerobic respiration using alternative terminal electron acceptors (e.g. sulfate, nitrate) or substrate-level phosphorylation.

aspects.label: Defense Against Reactive Oxygen Species
aspects.valueA: Produce catalase and/or superoxide dismutase to neutralize peroxide and superoxide byproducts.
aspects.valueB: Obligate anaerobes typically lack catalase/superoxide dismutase, leaving them vulnerable to oxidative damage.

aspects.label: Culture Conditions
aspects.valueA: Grown in ambient air or with added CO2; no special atmosphere needed for most.
aspects.valueB: Require anaerobic jars, chambers, or reducing media (e.g. thioglycolate broth) to exclude oxygen.

aspects.label: Clinical Context
aspects.valueA: Common in wound and respiratory infections exposed to air.
aspects.valueB: Associated with deep abscesses, necrotic tissue, and infections with a foul odor from fermentation byproducts.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Requires oxygen and can neutralize its toxic byproducts.
aspects.valueB: Cannot tolerate oxygen due to lack of protective enzymes.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: No catalase/SOD is the mechanistic reason anaerobes fear oxygen — not just habitat preference.
overlay.commonMisconception: "Anaerobic" doesn't mean weak or slow-growing — many anaerobes cause aggressive, foul-smelling infections.
